title: Rabban Bar Sauma's Journeys from Khanbaliq to Persia and Europe
intro: Rabban Bar Sauma, a Church of the East monk born in or near present-day Beijing, set out with his student Markos on a pilgrimage to Jerusalem. Danger on the routes turned them back to the Ilkhanate, and in 1287 he went to Europe as ambassador of Arghun, who wanted an alliance against the Mamluk Sultanate.
ending: Bar Sauma returned to Baghdad in 1288 with messages and gifts from the European leaders. The exchanges towards an alliance proved fruitless, and he died in Baghdad in 1294.

legs.title: The pilgrimage from China to Persia

stops.text: Bar Sauma was born in or near the site of present-day Beijing, then called Zhongdu and later Khanbaliq. In middle age he and his student Markos set out from Yuan China for Jerusalem.
stops.quote: Rabban ("monk" in Syriac) Bar Ṣawma was born c. 1220 in or near modern-day Beijing, known then as Zhongdu, later as Khanbaliq under Mongol rule.

stops.text: The two monks passed through the former Tangut country and then Khotan on the road west.
stops.quote: They traveled by way of the former Tangut country, Khotan, Kashgar, Taraz in the Syr Darya valley, Khorasan (now Afghanistan), Maragha (now Azerbaijan), and Mosul, arriving at Ani in the Kingdom of Georgia.

stops.text: Kashgar came next on the monks' route west, after the former Tangut country and Khotan.
stops.quote: They traveled by way of the former Tangut country, Khotan, Kashgar, Taraz in the Syr Darya valley, Khorasan (now Afghanistan), Maragha (now Azerbaijan), and Mosul, arriving at Ani in the Kingdom of Georgia.

stops.text: They crossed into the Syr Darya valley at Taraz, on the way towards Khorasan.
stops.quote: They traveled by way of the former Tangut country, Khotan, Kashgar, Taraz in the Syr Darya valley, Khorasan (now Afghanistan), Maragha (now Azerbaijan), and Mosul, arriving at Ani in the Kingdom of Georgia.

stops.text: The monks went on by way of Maragha, now in Azerbaijan, before turning to Mosul.
stops.quote: They traveled by way of the former Tangut country, Khotan, Kashgar, Taraz in the Syr Darya valley, Khorasan (now Afghanistan), Maragha (now Azerbaijan), and Mosul, arriving at Ani in the Kingdom of Georgia.

stops.text: Mosul was the last place named on the monks' route before they arrived at Ani in the Kingdom of Georgia.
stops.quote: They traveled by way of the former Tangut country, Khotan, Kashgar, Taraz in the Syr Darya valley, Khorasan (now Afghanistan), Maragha (now Azerbaijan), and Mosul, arriving at Ani in the Kingdom of Georgia.

stops.text: The monks arrived at Ani in the Kingdom of Georgia. Warnings of danger on the routes to southern Syria turned them from their purpose, and they went to the Ilkhanate in Persia instead.
stops.quote: Warnings of danger on the routes to southern Syria turned them from their purpose, and they traveled to Mongol-controlled Persia, the Ilkhanate, where they were welcomed by Patriarch Denha I of the Church of the East.

stops.text: Military conflict delayed the monks' return to China, and they stayed in Baghdad. When the Patriarch died, Markos was elected in his place as Yahballaha III in 1281.
stops.quote: The Patriarch then attempted to send the monks as messengers back to China, but military conflict along the route delayed their departure, and they remained in Baghdad. When the Patriarch died, Rabban Markos was elected as his replacement, Yahballaha III, in 1281.

stops.text: Bar Sauma crossed the Black Sea by boat to Constantinople, where he had an audience with Andronicus II Palaeologus. His writings describe the Hagia Sophia with enthusiasm.
stops.quote: then by boat to Constantinople, where he had an audience with Andronicus II Palaeologus. Bar Sauma's writings give a particularly enthusiastic description of the beautiful Hagia Sophia.

stops.text: Sailing to Italy, the ship passed Sicily, and Bar Sauma saw and recorded a great eruption of Mount Etna.
stops.quote: As their course took them past the island of Sicily, he witnessed and recorded the great eruption of Mount Etna on 18 June 1287.

stops.text: A few days after arriving, he watched a naval battle in the Bay of Sorrento between the fleets of Charles II and James II of Aragon. According to Bar Sauma, James II won and his forces killed 12,000 men.
stops.quote: A few days after his arrival, he also witnessed a naval battle in the Bay of Sorrento on St. John's Day, 24 June 1287, during the conflict of the Sicilian Vespers.

stops.text: Bar Sauma reached Rome too late to meet Pope Honorius IV, who had recently died. He negotiated with the cardinals instead and visited St. Peter's Basilica.
stops.quote: He next traveled to Rome, but too late to meet Pope Honorius IV, who had recently died. So Bar Sauma instead engaged in negotiations with the cardinals, and visited St. Peter's Basilica.

stops.text: On the way to Paris he stopped in Tuscany and the Republic of Genoa, and spent the winter in Genoa, a banking capital.
stops.quote: He spent the winter of 1287–1288 in Genoa, a famous banking capital.

stops.text: In France Bar Sauma spent a month with King Philip the Fair, who received the embassy favourably, gave him many presents and sent the nobleman Gobert de Helleville to accompany him back.
stops.quote: In France (Frangestan), he spent one month with King Philip the Fair, who seemingly responded positively to the arrival of the Mongol embassy, gave him numerous presents, and sent one of his noblemen, Gobert de Helleville, to accompany Bar Sauma back to Mongol lands.

stops.text: In Gascony, then in English hands, Bar Sauma met King Edward I of England, probably at Bordeaux. Edward was enthusiastic but could not join an alliance because of conflict at home with the Welsh and the Scots.
stops.quote: In Gascony in southern France, which at that time was in English hands, Bar Sauma met King Edward I of England, probably in the capital of Bordeaux.

stops.text: Back in Rome, the newly elected Pope Nicholas IV received him cordially and gave him communion on Palm Sunday. The Pope also entrusted him with a tiara for Mar Yahballaha.
stops.quote: Upon returning to Rome, Bar Sauma was cordially received by the newly elected Pope Nicholas IV, who gave him communion on Palm Sunday, 1288, allowing him to celebrate his own Eucharist in the capital of Latin Christianity.

stops.text: Bar Sauma returned to Baghdad in 1288 with messages and gifts from the European leaders. He lived there for the rest of his life and died in 1294.
stops.quote: Bar Sauma then returned to Baghdad in 1288, carrying messages and many other gifts from the various European leaders.

notes: The article dates none of the pilgrimage stops; they carry 'before 1281' (the year Markos was elected at Baghdad) and the year 1281 is a placeholder for ordering. The first stop's year is the birth year, not a departure date. Route from Baghdad to Constantinople is not given beyond Armenia and the Black Sea ('either Trebizond or Rum to Simisso'), so no stop between. Tangut country, Khorasan and Tuscany left out (regions). Maragha and Baghdad wp titles: Maragheh, Baghdad. 'Bay of Sorrento' uses Sorrento; the bay is not a separate article place. Gascony meeting is 'probably' at Bordeaux. Wp 'Khotan' may need check. Return to Rome also covers Gobert de Helleville joining; omitted.
